in_context.text: Paul would have liked to keep Onesimus with him in prison as a helper (1:13). But he would not do it without Philemon's consent. He wanted any kindness from Philemon to be freely chosen, not forced.

speaker.text: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, writing with Timothy.

audience.text: Philemon, Paul's fellow-worker, along with Apphia, Archippus and the church in his house.

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant, who had left him and become a believer through Paul.

what.text: Paul explains why he sent Onesimus back instead of keeping him. Paul could have commanded, but he chose to appeal for love's sake (1:8-9). Here he leaves the decision to Philemon so that his goodness would be willing.

events.text: During Paul's imprisonment, when Onesimus was being sent back to Philemon with this letter.

written.text: Traditional: about AD 60-62, from Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul wrote from prison; the letter does not name the city. It was sent to Philemon's household, traditionally at Colossae.

purpose.text: Paul wanted Philemon to act from his own free will, not because Paul pressured him. That is why he asks rather than orders.

big_picture.text: Scripture often values good done willingly over good done under pressure. Paul says the same about giving, "not grudgingly, or of necessity" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Peter tells elders to serve "not by constraint, but willingly" (1 Peter 5:2).

for_readers.text: Christian leaders are pictured as helpers, not lords over others' faith (2 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Peter 5:3). Good done freely and from the heart is what is sought.

why_it_matters.text: The word can mean mind, judgment, or counsel. The lexicon lists this verse under "counsel, advice." So "thy mind" here means Philemon's own judgment or consent.
It means necessity or compulsion. The same phrase "of necessity" is used in 2 Corinthians 9:7 about giving. Paul does not want Philemon's kindness to be forced.
It means voluntary, and in this phrase "of free will." The lexicon lists only this verse for it. It stands as the opposite of acting under necessity.

takeaway.text: Paul could have commanded, but he wanted Philemon's goodness to be his own free choice. Love asks and leaves room for a willing response.
